clue.text: Bans recitals – where this is played?

indicators.note: anagram indicator — the letters are 'played' with

explanation.walkthrough: The definition points back into the clue: 'where this is played?' asks for the instrument you would hear at those very recitals, so the fodder is also the scene of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Where this is played' asks what instrument such recitals happen on, and a bass clarinet is a genuine recital instrument, so the cryptic phrasing still names it straight.

clue.text: Basalt cracked with ice in chilly water

blocks.note: more fodder, mixed in with the rest

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a geology field note, and the trap is that it already sounds like chilly water — when a clue's plain meaning matches the answer's, you stop looking for letters to move.
explanation.definitionFit: The Baltic Sea is a real body of cold northern water, so 'chilly water' is a plain, factual description of the sea itself, not a play on words.

clue.text: Mum permits paddling here?

explanation.walkthrough: Every word works twice over: read straight it is a mother at the beach, read as wordplay it is silence plus permission, and the shallows really are where paddling is allowed.
explanation.definitionFit: Shallows are the paddling-depth water at a beach — exactly what a mum would allow a child to wade into, so the whole clue reads as a straight description.

clue.text: Vegetable, cold, resistant to the bite

blocks.note: c = cold, as on a tap

explanation.walkthrough: 'Vegetable, cold, resistant to the bite' reads like a gardener's note on a hardy crop, which is exactly what stops you seeing 'cold' as its one-letter abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Chard is a leafy vegetable, so 'Vegetable' names it by category — a definition by example, one member standing in for the whole class.

clue.text: Vegetable skill – I fail at a crucial moment

blocks.note: to choke = to fail under pressure

explanation.walkthrough: The happy accident is that an artichoke really does have a choke — the hairy heart you cut away — so the last piece of the charade is also part of the vegetable.
explanation.definitionFit: An artichoke is a vegetable too, so 'Vegetable' again names the answer by example rather than as an exact one-word synonym.

clue.text: Admired pair about to study carbon

blocks.note: a pair of ones — two Is
con is an old word for to study
C is the chemical symbol for carbon

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is two admirers signing up for chemistry together; the trap is 'pair', which is not people at all but simply the letter I written twice.
explanation.definitionFit: Iconic means revered as a symbol worth admiring, which is simply a stronger, more visual way of saying admired.

clue.text: Delete Times article finally

blocks.note: times = eras of history, not the newspaper

explanation.walkthrough: The capital T on 'Times' points hard at the newspaper, and the wordplay wants nothing of the sort — just plain eras, stretches of history.
explanation.definitionFit: Erase originally meant to rub or scrape a mark out, and that physical act is now used as the general, everyday synonym for delete.

clue.text: Applications supporting section of stage work

definitions.note: OPUSES is plural but the definition 'work' is singular, taken as a mass noun: a composer's 'work' means everything they wrote, which is exactly their opuses.

blocks.note: OP ('opposite prompt') is the side of a theatre stage opposite the prompter

explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'supporting' means sitting underneath rather than coming after. Across and down entries read position words differently, and this one only works pointing down. OP is theatre jargon for the side of the stage opposite the prompter.
explanation.definitionFit: An opus is a numbered creative work, most often musical, so a composer's opuses are simply their collected works under another name.

clue.text: Immediately agreeing to bring in Conservative

blocks.note: to be at one with someone is to agree

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is coalition horse-trading, which is why 'agreeing' reads as politics rather than as the phrase AT ONE waiting to be prised open.
explanation.definitionFit: 'At once' is the everyday phrase for happening without delay, which is exactly what 'immediately' means — a straightforward phrasal synonym.

clue.text: Old President leading America a dance

explanation.walkthrough: The surface borrows the idiom 'to lead someone a dance', so 'leading' looks like part of that phrase rather than an instruction about where to put the president.
explanation.definitionFit: A polka is one specific fast couple dance in duple time, so 'a dance' names the answer by example rather than by genre.

clue.text: Australian working with Australian in support for Nasa employee

blocks.note: the first Australian: A, as in A$
a strut is a support; ON A goes inside it

explanation.walkthrough: Two Australians for two As is the sly part: the same word clued twice, landing in two different places, so you go hunting for something more elaborate than a repeated letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Astronauts are the specific staff trained and sent into space by an agency like Nasa, so 'Nasa employee' pins down their job exactly.

clue.text: Went down the Cresta carrying child’s protective headgear?

blocks.note: you SLID down the Cresta Run toboggan track

explanation.walkthrough: Capitalised, Cresta looks like a place name in a holiday snapshot. The answer is biker slang, and it comes from the same idea — sliding when you would rather not.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Skid lid' is British slang for a motorcycle crash helmet, so 'protective headgear' describes its job while the question mark flags the slang.

clue.text: South American or Greek character offering little of profit

blocks.note: chi is the Greek letter χ

explanation.walkthrough: 'Offering little of profit' looks like an instruction to shorten a word, and it is nothing of the kind: it is a plain definition of LEAN.
explanation.definitionFit: A Chilean is a native of Chile, one specific nationality within South America, so the definition names the answer by geographic example.

clue.text: Source of light remains current in plant

blocks.note: a wind is a current of air
to plant seed is to sow; ASH WIND sits inside it

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads like a report from a factory — remains current in plant — and 'Source of light' for a window is the kind of sideways definition worth getting used to.
explanation.definitionFit: A sash window is what lets daylight into a room, so calling it a 'source of light' describes its function rather than naming it directly.

clue.text: Metal? You mined rocks, gaining mass

blocks.note: m = mass in physics, 'gained' by the fodder

explanation.walkthrough: 'You mined rocks' is exactly how you would come by the metal, and that is what makes the fodder invisible: it describes the answer while spelling it.
explanation.definitionFit: Neodymium is a specific rare-earth element that is indeed a metal, so 'Metal' names it by category, one example among many elements.

clue.text: Ready to complain after leader’s ousted

blocks.note: gripe = complain; its leader G is then ousted

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a party grumbling after a coup, and 'leader' does the same job in both readings: the head of a party, and the head of a word.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Ripe' extends beyond fruit to mean fully prepared or timed just right, which is precisely the sense 'Ready' carries here.

clue.text: I note that woman with sex-appeal and gold – recipient of legacy?

blocks.note: it = sex appeal, as in 'she's got it'

explanation.walkthrough: Five pieces in a row and not one instruction word — a pure charade. The leer at a woman in gold is there to keep you reading the clue as a sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: An inheritor is literally someone who receives an inheritance, so 'recipient of legacy' is a precise paraphrase of that legal role, not a stretch.

clue.text: They help one view fix over Church elevating Eastern philosophy

blocks.note: ZEN, 'elevating' — reversed upwards in this down entry

explanation.walkthrough: The bonus sits in the answer's own French: nez is nose, and a pince-nez pinches it. Both 'over' and 'elevating' are positional words that only work because this is a down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Pince-nez are glasses that clip to the nose, so wearing them literally helps one view things more clearly — a plain functional synonym.

clue.text: Go to bring in a salver

blocks.note: the A from the clue, brought inside

explanation.walkthrough: Read as an order to a servant it is one smooth sentence, and that hides the fact that 'Go' is a noun here — a go, a try — rather than the verb it looks like.
explanation.definitionFit: A salver is simply a formal, old-fashioned name for a flat serving tray, so the two words are near-exact synonyms, one plainer than the other.

clue.text: Parts swapped in Latin song from part of Italy

blocks.note: cantus is Latin for song, as in cantus firmus

explanation.walkthrough: Not the usual full jumble: 'Parts swapped' means two chunks changing places, CAN and TUS. Worth spotting when an anagram refuses to come out — sometimes only the halves move.
explanation.definitionFit: Tuscan means belonging to Tuscany, a region of Italy, so 'from part of Italy' is simply a paraphrase of the region's own adjective.

clue.text: Alluring? Happen to have success with leading man (not love)

blocks.note: to come to pass = to happen
HERO, the leading man, minus O — 'love' in tennis

explanation.walkthrough: The pieces divide as COME-HIT-HER, which is not how the answer reads at all. And 'love' for O comes from tennis, one of the handful of ways a setter can clue nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: A come-hither look is a classic idiom for an inviting, seductive glance, so 'Alluring' names its everyday sense directly.

clue.text: Concerned with Muslim leader rejecting an outcome

blocks.note: re = concerning, as in memo headers

explanation.walkthrough: 'Rejecting' sounds as though it should reverse something; here it simply throws letters away, and the news-bulletin surface keeps you thinking about the man rather than his title.
explanation.definitionFit: A result is simply what follows from an action, which is exactly what an outcome is — a direct, everyday synonym pair.

clue.text: Beautiful spot to get hot Javanese food

blocks.note: the Vale of Tempe in Greece, a classical byword for beauty
h = hot, as on a tap

explanation.walkthrough: The Vale of Tempe is worth filing away — setters reach for it whenever they want a beauty spot — and the holiday-brochure surface gives no hint that the answer is a soybean cake.
explanation.definitionFit: Tempeh is a fermented soybean cake that originated on Java, so 'Javanese food' names its true regional origin, not a loose guess.

clue.text: A lot of mud, intensely gleaming

blocks.note: 'A lot of' SILT — all but its last letter

explanation.walkthrough: 'A lot of' is the indicator to learn here: most of a word, not all of it. The surface, a muddy field described with feeling, gives nothing away about gleaming.
explanation.definitionFit: Silvery describes a bright, metallic sheen like polished silver, which is exactly the shining quality 'gleaming' points at.

clue.text: Only rich seen around this theatre?

explanation.walkthrough: A hidden word whose cover story does the hiding: 'seen around' sounds like gossip about who frequents the place, and the place is the Lyric — Hammersmith, or the West End.
explanation.definitionFit: The Lyric is a real theatre's actual name, in Hammersmith or the West End, so 'this theatre' identifies a specific proper noun, not a description.

clue.text: No longer suppresses scorn – UK’s struggling

blocks.note: more fodder, mixed in with the rest

explanation.walkthrough: 'No longer suppresses' looks too loose to be a definition until you think of uncorking your feelings rather than a bottle. Then it is exact.
explanation.definitionFit: To uncork is to let something pent-up burst free, so 'no longer suppresses' describes that same release, extended from bottles to feelings.

clue.text: No place to steal from subordinate

blocks.note: pl = place, as on street maps; 'No place' removes it

explanation.walkthrough: 'No place' reads as moral disapproval — nowhere is fit to steal from — and that is what disguises it as an instruction to delete two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Being 'under' someone in an organisation means being their subordinate, so the preposition and the noun describe the same rank relationship.

clue.text: Moved fast after active harbour regressed, becoming degenerate

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a port town in decline, which is the same story the answer tells. 'Regressed' is the reversal word: in an across clue it means backwards, right to left.
explanation.definitionFit: To atrophy is to waste away through disuse, which is precisely what 'becoming degenerate' describes — a decline in condition or strength.

clue.text: Describing birth name in any way? Not entirely

blocks.note: AT ALL = in any way; 'Not entirely' trims the final L

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like a question on a form, and 'Not entirely' is the giveaway — a phrase that merely qualifies the sentence on the surface, but underneath tells you to drop a final letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Natal is the adjective form of birth, as in 'prenatal' or a natal chart, so it literally describes anything to do with being born.

clue.text: Wild shamrock Portuguese islands twice cut down, reducing unnecessary quantities

blocks.note: the AZORES, 'twice cut down' — losing their last two letters

explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the principle stated properly: entities are not to be multiplied beyond necessity. The clue then enacts it, cutting the Azores down before shaving the whole thing into shape.
explanation.definitionFit: Ockham's razor is the principle of shaving away needless assumptions, so 'reducing unnecessary quantities' restates its own famous formula in plainer words.
